etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English forth, from Old English forþ, from Proto-West Germanic *forþ, from Proto-Germanic *furþą, from Proto-Indo-European *pŕ̥-to-, from *per-. Cognate with Dutch voort. See also ford.

definitions.definition: Forward in time, place or degree.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1604 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Othello, the Moore of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene ii], page 159:
quote.text: From this time forth, I never will speak word.

quote.citation: 1709-1725, John Strype, Annals of the Reformation in England:
1918, W[illiam] B[abington] Maxwell, chapter XIII, in The Mirror and the Lamp, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: “ […]  They talk of you as if you were Croesus—and I expect the beggars sponge on you unconscionably.” And Vickers launched forth into a tirade very different from his platform utterances. He spoke with extreme contempt of the dense stupidity exhibited on all occasions by the working classes.

definitions.definition: Out into view; from a particular place or position.

quote.citation: 1949, Joseph Campbell, “The Hero and the God”, in The Hero with a Thousand Faces:
quote.text: A hero ventures forth from the world of common day into a region of supernatural wonder:  […]

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Beyond a (certain) boundary; away; abroad; out.

quote.citation: c. 1596–1598 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merchant of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene v]:
quote.text: I have no mind of feasting forth to-night.

quote.citation: 1922, E[ric] R[ücker] Eddison, The Worm Ouroboros‎[1], London: Jonathan Cape, page 24:
quote.text: At the clashing of the cymbals the King sprang at Goldry as the panther springeth, and with the rush bare him backward and well nigh forth of the wrastling ground.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From fourth; compare forty.
